ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Processing of Anti-dumping duty cases 
*41. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per newspaper reports, normal time prescribed 
for processing Anti-Dumping Duty cases is 60 days, but actually the normal 
time taken by Commerce Ministry ranges between 12—20 months;  
(b) how many cases are pending with Government; and 
(c) how many cases have been settled, so far, and the time taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) No, Sir. As per the Anti -dumping rules the time prescribed for 
the completion of Anti -dumping investigations and recommending final 
findings after initiation is 12 months, extendable in exceptional circumstances 
by 6 months with the approval of the Central Government. The final 
determination has been recommended within 12 months in 25 cases out of 41, 
since the inception of action taken under the Anti -Dumping Rules. The 
extension from Central Government was taken in 16 cases under exceptional 
circumstances. A statement indicating details is at Annexure. [See Appendix 
189, Annexure No. 9] 
(b) and (c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(b) List of cases till date wherein the Designated Authority appointed under 
the Customs Tariff Acts and Rules made thereunder has recommended 
provisional Anti-dumping duty or where investigations have been initiated 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
and are pending for recommendations is given at Annexure [See Appendix 
189, Annexure No. 9] 
(c) List of cases till date where definitive duties have been recommended 
by the Designated Authority appointed under the Customs Tariff Acts and 
Rules made thereunder is given at Annexure. [See Appendix 189, Annexure 
No. 9] 
SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Mr. Chairman. Sir, in the changed regime 
of world trade that was in place under GATT, the countries who had been 
developing their industrial Base were to be protected through a measure of 
anti-dumpting duty. Sir, as a matter of fact, the reply given by the Government 
is not satisfactory at all. In addition to that, it is also a disappointing one. The 
normal time prescribed for taking a view on anti -dumping duty is 60 days. 
The Western countries, who are concerned only with their domestic industry, 
take a view in three or four months; whereas we in our country take almost 18 
months to take a view on anti-dumpling applications. I do not understand as to 
why such a long time is being taken by the authorities . 1 would like to know 
whether they are short of people or whether this is a motivated delay. The 
Government has not given me a proper reply on that account. Mr. Chairman, 
Sir, in the last eight years they have decided only 16 cases, whereas the 
number of applications fded with the Department is close to 57. I would like 
to know the reasons for such delays. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): Mr. Chairman, Sir, there is no 
cause for concern where India's init iating and following up the anti -dumping 
measure is concerned. I would like to correct the hon. Member's perception 
that we are slow in dealing with the anti -dumping cases. It is true that there is 
a prescribed measure whereby from the date the case is ini tiated, no action 
can be taken for 60 days. But that does not mean that action has to be taken on 
the 60th day. All that is means is that you cannot take action before the 
conclusion of the 60th day. As far as average of the Western countries is 
concerned, the average for the European Union and the United States of 
America ranges from six to seven months. 
As far as India is concerned, the average is seven to eight months. The 
time-frame that has been allotted to the Ministry of Commerce, to investigate 
anti-dumping cases, is twelve months. The Ministry may take extension under 
exceptional circumstances. I would like to inform the House that in the last 
2 

[28 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
year i.e., 1999, we had not sought, even in a single case, extension und er 
exceptional circumstances. We are hopeful that even in the current year —2000—  
we will not be asking for any extension under exceptional circumstances. Which 
means, we will be completing all anti -dumping cases that have been initiated 
within twelve months, and we will continue to do so. 
Another thing which I want the hon. Member to keep in mind is, the 
American Departments and the European Union have more than 300 to 400 
personnel to initiate and follow -up the anti -dumping cases. But, whereas we, 
in India, are surviving with barely 11 to 12 personnel and, even then, we are 
able to complete cases, on an average, within seven to eight months. 
SHRIPREM CHAND GUPTA: Sir, the reply given by the hon. Minister is 
not consistent with the statement laid by him. Si nce the beginning of 1992 till 
1998, only sixteen cases were decided and the average time taken was more 
than fifteen months. This is as per the reply of the Government. This is not my 
statement. How can he say that the Government is taking only six to seven 
months? It is not correct. The correct thing is, it is from thirteen to eighteen 
months. My submission is, it is not a question whether we take thirteen months 
or fourteen months or fifteen months or eighteen months. The question is, 
why do we want to delay? Mr. Chairman, Sir, there is a designated authority 
in the Ministry of Commerce which takes a view on the application filed 
before it by an industry. Thereafter, the application is sent to the Department 
of Revenue and they again take time. If this is  the case, what happens to that 
industry after eighteen months? After eighteen months, the industry becomes 
sick. Why are we taking more time? There must be some reason. 
My second supplementary is, we have a very strange system. We have a 
concept of NIP i.e., Non-Injurious Price, being determined by the designated 
authority. This practice is there only in India and nowhere else. Our decision-
makers say that since we have a lower cost of production, it does not harm the 
industry. Sir, in today's world, where  is the manpower involved in industry? 
Most of the production is operated either by computers or robots. A very high 
and advanced technology is used in producing a product. The NIP is a defective 
concept. I would like to ask the hon. Minister as to why is this NIP concept 
only in this country and nowhere else. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I am not sure what the 
connection between the price and the question is. As per the information that 
has been supplied to me, the European Union and some other countries have a 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
lesser duty rule and hence, the NIP is taken only as per those rules and no 
other rules. 
SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Sir, my points... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: No. Your supplementaries are over. 
SHRI S. B. CHAVAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I found, there is no co-ordination 
between the Ministries. I have got a letter. I have been raising the question 
about sugar import policy from Pakistan for the last four years. I got the latest 
letter from Shri Shanta Kumar, the Minister of Pu blic Distribution. He wrote 
to me stating that it is for the Ministry concerned to invoke the provisions of 
the Anti-Dumping Act. Is the hon. Minister aware of the fact that there is a 
huge amount of subsidy which is being given by Pakistan and other count ries 
from where either sugar or wheat is being imported? Sir, in spite of the fact 
that this question is being raised on the floor of the House for the last four 
years, I still get a reply that anti- dumping measure is not the responsibility of 
the Ministry  of Public Distribution; it is the responsibility of Commerce 
Ministry. There has to be some kind of a coordination between the two 
Ministries. So, I would like to know from the Commerce Ministry as to why, 
in spite of knowing fully well that a huge amount  of subsidy is being given to 
exporters in other countries, and there is no level playing field for the domestic 
industry, nothing is being done. The domestic industry is suffering a terrible 
loss, and in spite of raising the question all the while, I am not getting a proper 
reply. Now, I would like to know from the hon. Minister as to what is being 
done in this matter. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, through you, I would like 
to inform the hon. Member that there is a very strict procedure for initia ting 
anti-dumping measures, but the initiative cannot be taken by the Commerce 
Ministry. Even if there is a case, where action needs to be taken, the case must 
be put before the designated authority by the aggrieved industry, which means, 
the sugar industr y must make out a case to the designated authority and only 
then the anti-dumping measures can be initiated. So, I would request, through 
you ...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI S. B. CHAVAN: Everything is known to you. Questions regarding 
this are raised on the fl oor of the House ; and in spite of knowing fully well 
that this anti -dumping measure is absolutely necessary, you do not want to 
take any action. It clearly shows that there is some motive behind the whole 
thing. 
4 

[28 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: We have levied 60% duty on imported sugar 
to protect our industry, but since this question pertains to anti -dumping 
measures, all I can do is to request the hon. Member to use his good offices 
and ask the sugar industry to make out a case to the  Commerce Ministry. The 
Commerce Ministry would be more than happy to pursue it, but we cannot 
initiate the action. 
SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Sir, ...(Interruptions)...

SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the time -frame that has 
been prescribed is not the minimum, it is the maximum. If a stronger case is 
made out before the designated authority, lesser time would be taken in 
initiating the necessary action. It all depends on what sort of a case is made by 
the aggrieved industry. As far as the time frame is concerned, that is prescribed 
by the WTO. It is not done by rules framed by the Government of India. 
Therefore, to change this rule, all the countries within the W TO would have 
to agree to change this rule. 
SHRI JIBON ROY: With the signing of the WTO, it was expected that our 
exports and our overall trade would grow, but they are declining. From the 
date of signing the WTO, our exports have gone down from 28 per cen t to 4 
per cent. I wish to know how much the anti-dumping assault by foreign countries 
» has contributed to this reduction of exports. Very recently, Canada and the 
USA not only imposed anti -dumping regimes against us but they have also 
impounded our two s teel consignments. I wish to know what retaliatory anti-
dumping measures the Government has taken against these states in our country. 
The Minister himself has agreed that there was no inter -ministcrial 
coordination. The Minister himself has agreed that on ly 12 or 13 officials are 
working in such an important area. We wish to know what positive steps the 
Government has taken to stop it and to protect the interests of our industries 
in foreign countries. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Chairman, may I correct this? 
Unfortunately, words have been put into my mouth. I have at no stage said 
that there was no coordination. There is coordination. ...(Interruptions) 
SHRI JIBON ROY: You said that. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: When did I say that? I said that the sugar 
lobby must make a case to the Ministry of Commerce. I said nothing about the 
Ministry of Public Distribution. The Ministry of Public Distribution cannot 
make a case. The industry must make a case, not the Ministry of Public 
Distribution. 
As far as anti-dumping measures initiated against India are concerned; that 
is a separate question. If the hon. Member wishes to frame it, I will be happy 
to answer it at that stage. 
6 

[28 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: The sugar industry people must have 
met the Prime Minister at least three times. They must have met the Minister 
at least once. They have told them that sugar was being imported into the 
country from Beijing and Pakistan and that something should be done about 
the matter. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: As I have already mentioned, we have already 
raised the duty on imported sugar to 60 per cent. However, as far as anti -
dumping measures are concerned, meeting the Minister or meeting the Prime 
Minister is not good enough for a quasi-judicial authority like the Anti-Dumping 
Authority to initiate a case. The case must be made by the sugar industry to 
the designated Authority, and the necessary procedure will be carried out. 
SHRI S.R. BOMMAI: Is the Government aware that as sugar factories has 
stopped purchasing sugarcane from farmers, the farmers throughout the country 
are burning their sugarcane crops? Farmers have gone on hunger strikes. Some 
farmers have committed suicide in Karnataka because sugar factories did not 
receive their sugarcane. The sugar factories say that they have lakhs of tonnes 
of sugar in store and that they are not permitted to sell it. Under these 
circumstances, why is the Government importing sugar from Pakistan or any 
other counuy? I would like to know this. 
SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH: Mr. Chairman, t he Government is not 
importing sugar. 
Secondly, as I have already said more than once in my answer, as far as 
anti-dumping measures are concerned, the aggrieved industry must make a 
case. I will reiterate this again that as far as anti -dumping measures are  
concerned, the aggrieved industry must make a case. I would request the hon. 
Member to use his good offices to get the industry make a case to the designated 
Authority. We will take the necessary anti -dumping measures against the 
country that is dumping its products here. 
SHRI S.R. BOMMAI: I did not ask about anti -dumping measures. They 
are dumping the farmers. I would like to know whether they would stop it.

MR.CHAIRMAN: Question No. 43. 
Clearance of Revised Script of Film 'Water' 
*43. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that he himself had cleared the revised script of film 
'Water'; 
(b) if so, whether the suspension of permission for shooting of the film on 
the basis of this script can be construed as the breach of the fundamental right 
of freedom of expression; 
(c) if so, whether Government have taken it up with the Home Ministry for 
rectifying the situation; 
(d) if so, the response thereto; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING AND MINISTER OF STATE OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN JAITELY): (a) to (e) 
A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (e) The proposal for grant of permission for shooting the film "Water" 
by M/s Flagship International Limited from Canada was approved by this 
Ministry according to procedure prescribed for shooting in India, either wholly 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
or partly by foreigners, which is laid down in the Visa Manual of the Ministry 
of External Affairs. Permission was granted to the company by letter of 6th 
January 2000 after due consultation with Ministry of Home Affairs. 
The State Government of Uttar Pradesh conveyed that there were protests 
by organizations and persons in Varanasi about the content of the script and 
suggested re -examination of the script by the Go vt, of India. As per the 
procedure prescribed for shooting of feature films in India by foreigners, any 
material deviations in the approved script require prior permission of this 
Ministry. Accordingly, Ms. Deepa Mehta approached the Ministry for approval 
of a revised version of the script with certain amendments/deletions and 
dialogues in Hindi. Approval of the Government was accorded to the amended 
version on 2.2.2000. Shooting was resumed on 5th February but due to 
continued demonstrations by several org anizations and groups of persons 
causing a law and order problem in the city, the District Administration ordered 
stoppage of shooting for 15 days under Section 144 of Cr. PC by their order of 
7th February, 2000. 
Permission is granted by this Ministry to the applicant subject to a condition 
that shooting on locations would be with the permission of respective controlling 
authorities. As the permission to shoot in Varanasi is subject to the District 
Administration's permission, this Ministry has not approach ed the Home 
Ministry in this regard.

293. SHRI RAMACHANDRAIAH RUMANDLA: Will the Minister of

stocks; and

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) and (b) As per the current EXIM Policy exports of tobacco are 
free and are undertaken by exporters in both public and private sectors. All 
attempts are being made to help liquidate the stocks with the State Trading 
Corporation who has already floated a global tender in this regard. As the bulk 
of tobacco exports are against rupee payment by Russia, the Government of 
India have asked the Russian Authorities to allocate sufficient rupee funds to 
the Russian cigarette factories on credit terms to enable them to purchase 
Indian tobacco. An Indian delegation would visit Russia shortly to pursue the 
matter and to explore opportunities for greater cooperation between the tobacco 
industries of the two countries. 
Some of the steps taken to enhance export of tobacco, inter-alia, include:

international needs i.e., encouraging production of low tar, low 
nicotine and light soil tobaccos and discouraging production in 
undesireable soils.

standards. 
(v) Allowing exports of tobacco to Russia through "Debt Repayment

Agreement between America and India to remove restrictions 
†308. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA:                                       
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that an agreement has been entered into between 
America and India recently to the effect that all the restrictions imposed on 
India, so far, will be removed by 1st April, 2001; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that as per the agreements of World Trade 
Organisation these restrictions are to be removed by the year 2003; 
(c) if so, the reasons for removing these restrictions two years earlier; and 
(d) the expected benefits to be accrued to the country? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MARAN): (a) to (d) India has been maintaining Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) 
on imports for Balance of Payments (BOP) reasons. In January 1997, following 
an improvement in its BOP position the "Committee on BOP Restrictions" of 
the World Trade Organisation (WTO) invited India to present a phase out Plan 
for elimination of its remaining QRs maintained for BOP purposes. India 
presented a nine year phase out plan for removal of its QRs, which was further 
reduced to seven years but even this was not acceptable to a number of India's 
trading partners. Consequently, the Committee concluded its consultations 
without any decision. 
Subsequently, India held consultations and signed bilateral agreements with 
Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Switzerland, European Union and Japan for 
a six year phase out of its QRs on BOP grounds by 31.3.2003. However, such 
consultations with USA did not fructify and the USA initiated a dispute against 
India in the WTO. The Dispute Settlement Panel and the Appellate Body ruled 
against India holding that India was not justified in maintaining its QRs on 
BOP grounds. Following adoption of these reports by the Dispute Settlement 
Body (DSB), a Reasonable Period of Time (RPT) had to be determined for 
India to implement the ruling s and recommendations of the DSB. The RPT 
can be determined either through arbitration where the maximum period 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
normally granted is 15 months or through bilateral a greement between parties 
to the dispute. India and the USA have signed a bilateral agreement for 
determining the RPT, which would be of little over 18 months. As per the 
agreement, all the existing QRs on BOP grounds would have to be removed 
by 1.4.2001.

364. SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
SHRI GURUDAS DAS GUPTA: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the reported 
uncivilized acts of vandalism unleashed by the Sangh Parivar and the newly 
formed Kashi Sanskriti Raksha Sangharsh Samithi activists against the 
internationally acclaimed film Director, Deepa Mehta and her team and 
destroying the sets of film "Water" at Varanasi; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the sanction for the shooting of the film was obtained from his 
Ministry in advance; and 
(d) if so, why such attack on the shooting set in and Government's reaction 
thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING AND MINISTER OF STATE OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a), (b) 
and (d) On 31st January, 2000 Government of Uttar Pradesh conveyed that 
there were protests by sever al organizations and persons in Varanasi on the 
30th January, about the content of the script of the film "Water". The State 
Government informed that on the 30th January, 2000, a group of persons 
demonstrated on the location of the film during which some damage was caused 
to the sets prepared for shooting. There was no loss of life. In view of the 
protests, the State Govt, suggested re-examination of the script by the Govt, of 
India. A revised version of the script containing dialogues in Hindi with some 
deletions/modifications submitted by Ms. Deepa Mehta was approved by the 
Ministry on 2.2.2000. Shooting was done thereafter on 5th February, but due 
to a law and order problem created by the continued protests, demonstrations 
and an attempted suicide, the Di strict Administration ordered stoppage of 
shooting for 15 days under Section 144 Cr. PC by their order of 7th February, 
2000. 
(c) Yes Sir. The proposal of Canadian company, M/s. Flagship International 
Ltd. had been cleared for shooting of the film "Water" in India by the Ministry 
of Information and Broadcasting on 6.1.2000 according to procedure laid down 
in the Visa Manual brought out by the Ministry of External Affairs. Shooting 
of the film on location, however, is subject to permission of the respective 
controlling authorities.

 in India and submit its recommendations to the Government. The Committee,

ensure that every young worker bu.,ds up enough savings during his/her working

Steps to Implement the Disabilities Act, 1995 
390. SHRIRAMDAS AGARWAL:Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps Government have taken, till date, to implement the Persons 
with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full 
Participation) Act, 1995 so as to enable 60 milion disabled people in this 
country to lead a life of dignity and honour; 
(b) whether Government are aware that even the job quota of three per cent 
in Government jobs for the 'C and 'D' categories is not enough to do full 
justice to the capabilities of disabled people; and 
(c) if so, whether Government propose to impress upon public/private 
sector organisations to provide job opportunities to them? . 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATIMANEKA GANDHI): (a) A statement 
is laid on the Table of 4he House. (See below). 
(b) and (c) Keeping in view the necessity to provide job opportunities to 
the persons with disabilities, a provision has already been made under the 
Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full 
Participation) Act, 1995k to provide not less than 3% of vacancies for persons 
with disability of which one per cent each shall be reserved for persons suffering 
from (i) blindness or low vision; (ii) hearing impairment; and (iii) locomotor 
disability or cerebral palsy, in the posts identified for each disability, in the 
estabilsihments of every appropriate Government. The Act further provides 
under Section 41 that appropriate Governments and the local authorities shall, 
within the limits of their economic capacity and development, provide 
incentives to employers 1 both in public and private sectors to ensure that at 
least five per cent of their work force is composed of persons with disabilities. 
The Ministry of SJ & E, in accordance with the provision, has requested the 
Ministry of Finance to initiate appropriate action in this regard. 
Statement 
The Persons w ith Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights 
& Full Participation) Act, 1995, enacted and enforced from Feb., 1996 is an 
important landmark in Government of India's efforts to ensure equal 
opportunites for persons with disabilities and their full participation in nation-
building. It provides for both preventive and promotional aspects of 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
rehabilitation like education, employment and vocational training, job 
reservation, research and manpower development, creation of barrier -free 
environment, rehabilitation for persons with disability, unemployment 
allowance for the disabled, special insurance scheme for disabled employees 
and establishment of homes for persons with severe disability etc. 
The implementation of the provisions of the Act, requires a multi -sectoral 
collaborative approach, of all Ministries of the Central Government, the State 
Governments and other appropriate authorities. They have all been requested 
to take necessary action expeditiously. The f ollowing actions have been taken 
to implement various provisions of the Act: 
(a) The National Handicapped Finance & Development Corporation has 
been operationalised with effect from 24.10.97 to support 
entrepreneurial activity by the disabled. 
(b) Notification of Central Co -ordination Committee as per Section 3 of 
the Act. The Committee has undertaken two meetings so far. 
(c) Central Executive Committee.has been notified. The Committee took 
four meetings so far to review the progress of implementation of the 
Act. 
(d) The C hief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities has been 
appointed and he has assumed the office w.e.f. 1.9.98. 
(e) Five Core Groups of experts and relevant Ministries have been set up 
to make recommendations and formulate schemes to give effect to 
various provisions of the Act. 
(f) 3% reservation of jobs in Government establishments and Public Sector 
Undertakings has been provided under the Persons with Disabilities 
(Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 
1995, for the persons with disabilities. 
(g) The Ministry has set up an Expert Committee under the Chairmanship 
of Additional Secretary (SJ & E), to review the existing identification 
of posts (done in 1986) and to identify more suitable posts. 
(h) Rules under section 73(1) and (2) have been notified. 
(i) The National Fund for People with Disabilities, which was set up under 
134 

[28 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the Charitable Endowment Act, 1890 on 11.8.1983, has been activated 
and assistance has been sanctioned to non -government agencie s. So 
far, 17 Projects have been sanctioned under the Scheme. 
(J) A new   Scheme, namely, Viklang Bandhu has been formulated to 
provide   training to disabled volunteers. The National Institutes and     
Regional Rehabilitation Training Centres have so far trained a number 
of Viklang Bandhus. 
(k) A Bill for setting a National Trust for the welfare of persons with 
Autism, Cerebral Palsy. Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities 
has been passed to provide support to these vulnerable categories and 
their families. 
(1) The Rehabililation Council of India, which is statutory body for 
standardisation and training of rehabilitation professional, recognition 
of training institutions and registration of professionals, has recently 
taken up a plan for man -power in disability rehabilitation throughout 
the country. Funds have been allocated to RCI for this purpose. 
(m) Most State Governments have constituted Slate Coordination 
Committee and State Executive Committee and have appointed 
Commissioner for Persons with Dis abilities, to redress the grievances 
of the disabled persons. 
(n) A Scheme called National Programme for Rehabilitation of Persons 
with Disabilities has now been approved for establishing necessary 
infrastructure Up to the District level, to realise fully the objectives of 
the Act. Funds are being released to the State Governments for 
implementation of the Scheme. 
(o) A Conference of State Secretaries, in-charge of persons with disabilities 
was held on 14 -15, Feb., 2000 at New Delhi to discuss the 
implementation of the Act. A Workshop of State Education Secretaries 
and State Labour Secretaries was also held at New Delhi to sensitise 
the State Officials and to monitor the progress of implementation of 
the Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights 
and Full Participation) Act, 1995. 
(p) An Inter-ministerial Group has been constituted to monitor the progress 
made by the Central Ministries who have specific obligations under 
the Act. 
 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
(q) Two Schemes are being implemented for providing support to non-
government agencies working for various programmes for rehabilitation 
of persons with disabilities, 
(r) In consonance with the policy of providing a complete'package of 
welfare services to the physically, mentally, hearing and visually 
handicapped individuals and groups and in order to effectively deal 
with the multidimensional problems of the handicapped population, 
the Ministry of SJ & E has established six National/Apex Institutes, 
each working in a spec ific area of disability. These institutes are apex -
level organisations in the field of education, training, vocational 
guidance, counselling, research, rehabilitation and development of 
suitable service modules for the disabled. 
(s) The Artificial Limbs Manufacturing Corporation (ALIMCO), Kanpur 
was established in November, 1972 as a Public Sector Company with 
the main objective of developing and manufacturing standard aids and 
appliances for the disabled persons and to make them available at 
reasonable pri ces to them throughout India. It manufactures wheel 
chairs, tricycle, aritificial limbs, crutches and many other aids and 
appliances for the handicapped persons. A scheme for setting up four 
Auxiliary Production Centres of ALIMCO has been launched recently  
with a view to expand the production base of ALIMCO. 
(t) The District Rehabilitation Centre Scheme (DRC) was initiated by the 
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment during 1985 to provide 
Comprehensive rehabilitation services to the rural disabled right at 
their door step in 11 districts of the country. Four Regional 
Rehabilitation Training Centres (RRTCs) have also been set up at 
Chennai, Mumbai, Cuttack and Lucknow for training and manpower 
development in the field of rehabilitation, particularly for the DRCs. 
(u) A programme viz. Rashtriy a Gramin Viklang Sahayata Samiti has been 
launched, under which 100 districts have been identified and selected 
to provide rehabilitation services in collaboration with the district 
authorities and the respective State Government. 
(v) A scheme for setting up four regional centres for the spinally injured 
and persons with orthopaedic disabilities have been recently approved 
for implementation as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with Centre:State 
share on 90:10 basis.

THE SMALL INDUSTRIES DEVELOPMENT BANK 
OF INDIA (AMENDMENT) BILL, 1999. 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHW ANT SINHA):Si r, I 
move: 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
"That the Bill to amend the Small Industries Development 
Bank of India Act, 1989, as passed by Lok Sabha, be 
taken into consideration." 
The Small Industries Development Bank of India is a development 
financial institution which was set up in 1990 as a wholly -owned subsidiary of 
IDBI for financing, promotion and development of the SSI sector and for 
coordinating the functions of other institutions associated with financing the 
SSI sector. SIDBI is responsible for providing long-term assistance to small 
scale industries and the working capital requirements are financed by 
commercial banks and other prime lending institutions. SIDBI has, so far, 
sanctioned assistance amounting to Rs.45,144 crores during the period 1990-
1999 and the disbursements during the period have been Rs.32,987 crores. 
To enable SIDBI to play a more effective role in the overall development of 
SSI sector and equip SIDBI to discharge its apex role in credit delivery to the 
SSI sector, I had proposed delinking of SIDBI from IDBI and transfer of IDBI 
shareholdings in SFC s to SIDBI in my Budget speech for 1998-99. 
Comprehensive amendments to the Small Industries Development Bank of 
India Act, 1989 proposed in the Bill seeks to delink SIDBI from IDBI, 
strengthen its capital structure and provide greater functional autonomy and 
operational flexibility to SIDBI. The main features of the proposed 
amendments are: enhance authorised capital of SIDBI from existing Rs.250 
crores to Rs. 1,000 crores with provision for further increase to Rs.2,000 
crores; enlarge shareholder base of SIDBI by allowing IDBI to transfer 
minimum fifty -one per cent of its equity holding in SIDBI in favour of public 
sector banks, insurance companies, etc.; enable SIDBI to offer 49 per cent of 
its equity to public; restructure the Board of Directors of SIDBI , and empower 
the Board to exercise full powers relating to borrowing, acceptance of deposits 
and investment of surplus funds; empower general body of shareholders for 
appointment of auditors, approval of annual accounts and approval of rate 
dividend; empower SIDBI to reduce its share capital with prior approval of the 
Government of India and to issue redeemable preference shares and convert 
part of existing share capital into redeemable preference shares. 
Sir, with these words, I request that this Bill be taken up for 
consideration and be passed. 
The question was proposed.

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
employment on local and regional basis. The growth of small scale industries is 
also a safeguard against monopolization of capital in a few hands. With the 
trend of liberalisation and globalisati on, the small scale sector has taken a 
beating. The reservation of goods for the small scale sector has been rendered 
a severe blow by the Government. On the other hand, the open invitation by 
the Government for foreign investment has also made the job of the SSIs 
difficult. The idea behind encouraging foreign investment was to ensure growth 
in core sector where the need for greater investment and better technology was 
felt. However, trends have shown that instead of investment in the core sector, 
the foreign direct investment is flowing into the consumer goods sector. The 
consumer sector where SSI has an important role to play is thus a sufferer. 
The multinational companies are liberally using foreign direct investment to 
finish the small scale sector units. Another point which deserves to be noted is 
with regard to the undesirable trends associated with the multinational 
companies which are bringing in foreign direct investment at the expense of 
the small scale sector. These multinational corporations have been bringing in 
outdated technology and their investment is mostly limited to second in 
machinery. They have entered the industrial scene on a fifty -fifty basis and 
then quickly they are trying to take the majority control. Their focus is also to 
take short-term gains than the long-term gains. Such undesirable features on

greater reliance on developing our own small scale sector units which has 
ushered in a cost effective manufacturing and which will have a long-term 
strategy. Unless the Government makes corrections in its policy directions 
towards these small scale industries, the growth of this sector cannot be 
ensured by only making SIDBI an autonomous body and by increasi ng the 
share base of this institution. Thank you.

with me - 10.3% in March, 1998, and it had gone up to 11% by  March, 1999. 
Sir, the other thing, I am sure, about which the House is aware, is the fact that 
whenever a bank, in whichever category, fails to give the required credit, i.e. 
40% , to priority sector, we pre-empt that money. We have a system by which 
we pre-empt that money, we place it at the disposal of SIDBI, we place it at the 
disposal of NABARD, and that money is then pumped into the priority sector 
through these routes. So, we will continue to review priority sector lending by 
the commercial banks, by all banks, and it will be our endeavour to ensure that 
not only the target of 40%, but well beyond that target is met by all these 
banks. 
As far as the North-East is concerned, I want to say that our 
commitment is very clear to the North-East, to the development of the North-
East.   Despite the fact that Mr. Khagen Das feels that I am not a 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
socialist any more, let me assure him that as far as the commitment to the 
North-East is concerned, socialism or no socialism, that  commitment 
continues. I have here figures of all the advances. ..(Interruptions) .... I do not 
know, Sir, when I was a socialist. I spent 24 hours in the bureaucracy, and the 
bureaucrat does not have an ideology. He is not supposed to be with this party 
or that party. 
During the period of nine years from 1990 to 1999, the SIDBI's 
cumulative sanction to the North-East was Rs.212 crores, and the 
disbursement was Rs.182 crores. There was a meeting recently taken in 
Shillong by the Prime Minister. I was also present in that meeting. The 
Government has reiterated its commitment to development of the North. -East. 
I will like to assure the House and the hon. Members that we shall be doing 
our best for the promotion of industries, especially small -scale industries,  in 
the entire North-East. 
As far as the overall lending to all the backward areas is concerned, 
it is a very satisfactory figure of 29 per cent by the SIDBI. 
Mr. Virumbi has raised the issue of mismatch between sanctions and 
disbursements. I want to say that there is always a mismatch. Let us not forget 
that the SIDBI is a refinance institution. It does not lend directly. It is a 
refinancing institution, and two -thirds of its funds are made available to the 
State Finance Corporations, through which refinancing takes place. Therefore, 
there will always be, as there indeed is in any financial institution, a mismatch, 
an apparent mismatch between sanctions and the actual disbursements. 
However, I think, the record of the SIDBI in this regard is satisfactory. 
The SIDBI runs 13 promotional schemes for the small -scale sector, 
and one of those schemes is promotion of technology. It has a technological 
promotion scheme. It has the Technology Development and Modernisation 
Fund, which the SIDBI runs for the small- scale sector. Then, it has a separate 
Technology Upgradation Fund for textile industries. These are the two 
schemes, through which the SIDBI is assisting in technology upgradation and 
modernisation. 
SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Its performance in 
technology development has not been good for the last three years. Whatever 
has been the target, it has always been behind that.  If that can be 
206 

[28 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
improved, that will help small -scale industries. Unless small -scale industrie s 
develop the technology, it will not be possible for them to compete. 
SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: I entirely agree with the statement that the 
small-scale industry has to strengthen itself in various areas, and technology is 
certainly one. We are doing all we ca n to promote technology. However, when 
we are dealing with a finance institution, let us remember that there is demand 
and there is supply. I suggest that it is the responsibility of all of us to 
encourage the units in the small -scale sector to take advant age of the funds 
that are at the disposal of the SIDBI for modernisation and technology 
development. I am quite sure that if all of us together carry awareness to the 
SSI sector, it will be able to take advantage of the various windows that are 
available with the SIDBI for this purpose. 
I suggest that this piece of legislation that I have brought before the 
House, that the Lok Sabha has already considered and passed, is a 
progressive piece of legislation. It will indeed go a long way in promoting the 
interests of the SSI sector. I, therefore, suggest that the House adopt this Bill 
with acclaim. 
Thank you, Sir.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
Failure of Government of India to Prevail upon Gujarat Government to 
withdraw Circular Removing the Ban on its Emmployees Participating 
in R.S.S. Activities. 
DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, I rise' to 
raise a discussion on the failure of the Government of India to discharge its 
constitutional responsibility to protect secularism which is one of the basic 
tenets of the Constitution of India by not prevailing upon the State Government 
of Gujarat to withdraw the circular removing the ban imposed on the State 
Government employees in participating in the activities of the R.S.S. 
Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, ours is a system of Parliamentary 
democracy. Secularism is also a basic tenet of our polity, and I submit to you 
that the safeguarding of parliamentary democracy and the secular values 
requires that the civil services in our country should be totally neutral when it 
comes to political affiliations. I recall, when the role of civil services was being-
discussed in the Constituent Assembly in 1948 or 1949, Sardar Patel had 
warned the country that if the political neutrality of our services is not ensured, 
then we will have a system of administration which will not be able to 
implement the constitutional scheme of things which the Assembly was then 
debating.   . 
. Sir, for the successful functioning of our  parliamentary democracy, for 
the safeguarding of secular values which we all cherish, it is absolutely 
essential that our Civil Services should be seen to act in the most impartial 
manner. Political neutrality of our Civil Services, both at the Central and the 
State levels, is absolutely essential for the successful functioning of our 
system of parliamentary democracy. It is in this context, Sir, that I note with 
deep sorrow the attempts now being made to destroy this basic edifice of a 
politically neutral Civil Service which, I believe, has served our country very well 
thus far. Sir, I do not want to go into the history of the RSS, nor do I want to 
use any harsh words. In the RSS, there are people like the hon. Shri Nanaji 
Deshmukh. He is a person whom I greatly respect, but, Sir, to put it very 
mildly, the RSS remains a highly controversial organisation. We all know the 
circumstances in which the RSS was banned after the assassination 
210 

[28 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of Mahatma Gandhi, and the events of those days are vividly described in a 
book which was authored by Shri Pyare Lal, the then Secretary of Mahatma 
Gandhi. In that book, quoting Gandhiji, he described the RSS as a communal 
organisation, with a totalitarian outlook. Sir, we know when the RSS  was 
banned, there were negotiations between the Government and the authorities 
of the RSS, and, after that, the ban was lifted. For the first time, 1 believe, 
RSS had a written constitution and, if I read correctly, article 4 of its 
constitution states th at "the Sangh has no politics and is devoted to purely 
cultural work". And it is further stated in that article: "In consonance with the 
cultural heritage of the Hindu Samaj, the Sangh has abiding faith in the 
fundamental principle of tolerance towards all  faiths." Sir, we all know, and I 
say it with great regret, that the Sangh has not lived up to these commitments. 
Its role in fanning communal strife has been documented by many 
Commissions of Inquiry; and, in this context, Sir, I draw your attention to th e 
Report of the Jaganmohan Reddy Commission on Ahmedabad Riots (1969, 
the Report of the Madan Commission on Bhiwandi Riots (1970), Justice 
Vithayathil's Report on Tellfcherry Riots (1971), Justice Jitendra Narain's 
Report on Jamshedpur Riots (1979) and Jus tice P. Venu Gopal's Report on 
Kanyakumari Riots (March, 1982). Sir, we all know that although the RSS 
describes itself as a socio-cultural organisation, in practice, it makes no 
distinction between culture and politics. 
If you read the Organiser, or, the other organs of the RSS, there is 
nothing but politics in all those papers. The Sarsanghchalak, Shri Rajendra 
Singh, some years ago, came out with a scheme for amending the Constitution 
in a most fundamental form. And in this background, Sir, it is most unfortunate 
that the hon. Prime Minister has chosen to describe the RSS as a purely cultural 
organisation. I think that is the biggest joke of this century. The worst part is 
that what the Gujarat Government has done, the Central Government seems to 
have abetted it and encouraged it to remove the ban on the RSS. We know that 
the Gujarat circular talks of a circular issued by the Government of India dated 
13th July, 1999. And in this circular, the Central Government seems to have told 
the Gujarat Government that the RSS is not a banned organisation. That 
certainly is true. It is true that after the demolition of the Babri Masjid, the RSS 
was declared unlawful, and that was set aside by the Justice Bahri Commission 
under the Unlawful Activities Act. But the ban on Government servants joining 
the RSS was imposed long before that. And that ban on non-participation of 
Government servants in the activities of 
211 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
Jamat-i-Islami and the RSS was as a result of totality of considerations  which 
weighed with the Government from time to time about the activities of these 
organisations. To say that an organisation is not illegal, in my humble opinion, is 
not a sufficient proof that it is a fit organisation for the Government servants to 
participate. No recognised political party is illegal. And, yet, no civil servant can 
join any recognised political party. Therefore, Sir, the Gujarat Government, 
taking advantage of this circular of 13th July, 1999, has done a thing which is 
totally unacceptable to us. In fact, Sir, in the interest of transparency, we would 
like the hon. Home Minister to place on the Table of this House the 
correspondence between him and the Gujarat Government, the exchange of 
letters; the letters on the basis of which the Gujarat Government has removed 
the ban on the RSS. If the logic of the hon. Home Minister is followed, I think 
that logic will lead him to remove the ban on the Central Government 
employees also participating in the activities of the RSS. Therefore, Sir, I 
submit that the hon. Home Minister should enlighten us about this exchange of 
letters between the Home Ministry and the Gujarat Government which form the 
basis of the decision taken by the Gujarat Government. Sir, the fact that the 
RSS is not merely an ordina ry cultural, or, social organisation is not a new 
thing because this debate has been going on in our country for many, many 
years. I recall, for example, when the Janata Party Government was in power in 
the late 1970's, several non-BJP Members of that coal ition had raised that 
issue. The dual membership issue was precisely an issue that the RSS is, for 
all practical purposes, a political organisation and cannot be equated to a 
merely social and cultural organisation. For all these reasons, Sir, what the 
Gujarat Government has done amounts to, in my humble view, an attempt to 
subvert the essential purpose of our Constitution. And the RSS, within public 
administration, whether in Delhi, or, in Gujarat, in my humble view, cannot 
serve the secular Constitution w hich we all cherish. For all these reasons, I 
feel, it is the bounden duty of the Central Government to advise the Gujarat 
Government to reconsider this matter. Unfortunately, what the hon. Prime 
Minister has stated has encouraged some other State Governme nts, like UP 
and Himachal Pradesh, to say that they also propose to follow the footprints of 
the Gujarat Government. I sincerely feel it is still not too late for the Central 
Government to appreciate the gravity of the situation and do the right thing to 
protect, in letter and spirit, the Constitution and public administration of our 
country. 
212 

[28 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, it may be argued that what the Gujarat Government has done is 
merely a State subject. I don't want to go into the Constitutio nal niceties. But 
what the Gujarat Government has done has wide ramifications for the 
functioning of public administration in our country. If the lead of the Gujarat 
Government is followed by the Governments of UP, Himachal Pradesh and 
other States, I thin k: that would constitute a serious subversion of the 
Constitution of India and, therefore, I feel it is the bounden duty of the Central 
Government to intervene in this matter. 
Sir, I recall, some two or three years ago, the Maharashtra 
Government had decided to wind up the Srikrishna Commission. But the hon. 
Prime Minister at that time intervened, and in his wisdom he found it necessary 
to advise the Maharashtra Government not to implement that decision. 
Similarly, we feel, Sir, this is a grave issue which demands and calls for the 
intervention of the Prime Minister and the Government of India to protect and 
safeguard the Constitution of India. 
Sir, it is my honest conviction that a public administration ridden with 
RSS can neither serve our parliamentary system of Government, nor can it be 
expected to protect the secular values which we all cherish. Thank you.

discussion on this issue and I would like the House and the Government to

THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN : Now, the matter is that he wants a 
discussion in the House. I will look into both the records and then I will give 
my ruling. Just now, let the discussion go on because in this controversy 
"whether he said it, he did not say it,  it came in the newspaper, whether a 
circular is there or not", nothing can be said. It can be checked later. Now, 1 
will ask Shri Ramachandran Pillai to speak. 
SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLAI (Kerala) : Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, the Leader of the Opposition has raised an important issue. After 
the assumption of - power by the B.J.P. at the Centre, a deliberate organised 
attack is there against the secular and democratic polity of our country. This 
attack is extended to all secular and democratic institutions in our country. The 
manner of attack is two-pronged. One, there is a direct frontal attack against 
the institutions. There is an attempt of infiltration and trying to sabotage from 
within. This is the second type of attack that is being done. Madam, sectarian, 
intolerant and aggressive Hindu communal policies are being patronised under 
the B.J.P. rule in this country, and these attempts have created a very 
dangerous situation, not only to the democratic and secular polity of our 
country, but also to the very existence of the integrity and unity of our nation. 
Madam, lifting of the ban on the Government employees joining R.S.S. in 
Gujarat and its justification by the Ministers at the Centre is not a simple 
matter. It is not only a question of allowing Governmen t servants joining 
political parties or engaging in political activities. This is not an isolated 
incidence. It is part of a process, it is part of a process of incidents taking 
place in this country ~ the attack against the filming of "Water" in Banaras, the 
withdrawal of books by the ICHR, the consistent attack against minorities and 
their institutions.   The argument of 
233 

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
the Gujarat Government and the argument raised by my hon. friend, Shri 
Ramdas Agarwal that R.S.S. i s a socio -cultural organisation is not based on 
facts. The R.S.S. has a distinct political philosophy of its own. It gives a very 
narrow definition of culture synonymous with religion and it gives an entirely 
different interpretation of Hinduism and trying to impose its views on others. 
They also ask others to submit to their views. They believe in establishment of 
a Hindu rashtra. and they are striving for it. If this is not politics, then, what is 
politics? The RSS is more political than the BJP, and there is no justification in 
saying that it is a socio- cultural organisation and that employees can join this 
organisation. 
Madam, I find that this philosophy of the RSS is dangerous to India's 
integrity and unity. If the RSS is patronised and if Government em ployees are 
persuaded and induced to join the RSS, this will have very serious 
repercussions for the secular, democratic polity of our country. 
Madam, India is a country of rich diversities. We speak different 
languages. We believe in different religions. Our lifestyles are different. We 
have different ethnic communities. We have different cultures. It is a fact that 
there is unity among this diversity. The common will to live together is there, 
and this is the strengthening. 
Madam, if we look back at India's history, we have withstood waves of 
immigrations and invasions in the past. All the people who came to India before 
the industrial revolution in west became part of India. All contribute to the 
richness of India's composite culture. What helped us in wi thstanding-the 
attacks of these invaders? The flexibility, the tolerance, the openness and the 
give-and-take attitude. That helped us to maintain the integrity and unity of 
India. 
The philosophy now patronised and propagated under the BJP 
Government is against India's interests. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh 
is arguing arid branding tolerance as an act of cowardice. It is branding 
openness and flexibility as anarchy and indiscipline. It works for sectarian, 
intolerant and aggressive policies. If employees  are allowed to join this 
organisation, if employees are encouraged to join this organisation, definitely 
the unity and integrity of our country will be in danger. This will also attract such 
trends in other social sections. The attempt of this sectarian group to hold the 
country to ransom should be definitely resisted.

RAJYA SABHA [28 February, 2000] 
I am glad that some of the partners of the National Democratic 
Alliance, particularly the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam and the Telugu Desam 
Party, have come out opposing the action of the Gujarat Government in 
allowing its employees to participate in activities of the Rashtriya 
Swayamsevak Sangh. I nope more of N.D.A. partners will come out and show 
more courage and determination in resisting the attempt of t he BJ.P. in 
patronising the sectarian policies and pratices. 
In the country the unity and integrity is now at stake. All patriotic 
forces should come forward unitedly to fight this drift, to fight these sectarian 
policies. The Central Government have to ab ide by the provisions of the 
Constitution and they are duty bound to protect the secular and democratic 
polity of the country. Instead of performing that act, they are encouraging 
those forces, which are attacking the secular aqnd democratic polity. Madam,  
all democratic forces shouid come forward to resist this attempt. 
With these words, I conclude.

SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh) : I 
thank you, Madam Deputy Chairman, for allowing me to participate in the 
Short Duration Discussion. 
There cannot be two opinions on the discharge of the Constitutional 
responsibility to protect secularism not only by the Government of India and 
the State Governments; it is also the responsibility of every patriotic citizen of 
the country. We have adopted the system of parliamentary democracy, in the 
best interests of our country. Different parties have come to power ,both in the 
Centre and in the States, but the administrative set -up continues. A person 
once appointed in Government service remains there for 25 to 30 years, i.e. till 
his retirement. The parties voted to power are accountable and answerable to 
the people. The parties, in power, are thrown out, or, are susceptible to be 
thrown out of power, whereas the bureaucracy is neither accountable, nor can 
it be thrown out of power. Hence, our Party is of the firm opinion that the 
persons who are part of the Administration should be neutral, and no person 
should be allowed to join an organisation having visible or invisible 
connections, or links with any political party of the country. 
Our Chief Minister has stated unequivocably that the Government of 
Andhra Pradesh will not allow any employee to join or associate himself with 
an organisation having links with political parties. We are also glad that our 
hon. Prime Minister has categorically stated that the Government of India 
employees will not be allowed to join an organisation having links with political 
parties. 
Madam, the discussion in the House pertains to the Gujarat State 
Government which has withdrawn the circular, removing the ban imposed on 
the State Government employees to participate in the activities of the RSS. 
We feel that the Government of India cannot be blamed for this act of the 
Gujarat Government. Sir, we cannot deviate from our stand that the 
Government of India should not exceed its limits while dealing with the States 
and should confine itself to the provisions of the Constitution and strive hard 
to protect and strengthen the federal structure but, at the same time, we are 
unable to accept that the RSS is not having  connections with any political

"You may kindly recall that of late, a controversy is being kicked up

Government of India have, in their rules specifically prohibited Government 
servants from joining political parties. Granting permission on the plea that an 
organisation is a social organisation will tend to open the Pandora's box. This

pretext of social character, to attract Government servants into their fold. 
Ultimately, it will affect the administrative structure nurtured over a period of time 
and make inroads into disciplined forces like the Polfce, the Defence and 
other important services. This will lead to unnecessary problems. The 
Government employees are bound by the Constitution and they are

that Government servants should not indulge in political activities and that the 
people should not lose faith in the impartial and apolitical functioning of the 
administrative machinery. We have many more important tasks in nation -
building. Our combined energies should not be frittered away on such 
contentious issues which may distract our attention as well as the attention of 
the people. I, very sincerely, feel that a consensus may be arrived at, 
forbidding the Government servants from joining social organisations having 
links with political parties. So, this letter has been addressed to the Prime

SHRI     BRAHMAKUMAR     BHATT     (Gujarat): Madam 
Vice-Chairman, I don't want to refer to Gandhiji's murder or Godse or such 
other things. I want to draw the attention of this House to certain facts which 
are on record. After the Gujarat Government removed the ban on Government 
servants, including bureaucrats, from joining the RSS, obviously, the Prime 
Minister, when he was on an election tour, was asked by the Press to comment 
on this. I myself saw it on T.V. In a very short reply, he has.said, "it is a cultural 
organisation". I would like to know from the hon. Prime Minister whether he 
considers RSS something like the Swadhyaya Parivar or something like the 
Ramakrishna Mission or any other cultural organisation of that type. If that is 
so, then the question will arise as to why the ban is continuing in the Central 
Government, if he considers it as a cultural organisation. Then, what prevents 
the Government of India from removing the ban in each State? That is the 
main question. Madam, the point that it must have been in the minds of those 
who are in power, "Yes, let Gujarat be a litmus test. Let us see what is 
happening there. Let us see what the reactions are from the people, from 
different political parties and from the alliance partners, and then we will t hink 
of proceeding further". -So, this 
whole thing has started from Gujarat. It is only when the alliance 
partners, namely, the DMK, the Samata and the TDP, pressurised the 
Government and openly told the Prime Minister through the Press and the 
electronic media that they don't agree with this and that they want the Gujarat 
Government to withdraw this circular, the hon. Prime Minister issued a circular 
and told the Press that so far as the Government of India is concerned, the 
ban continues. This is the position. 
Madam, now, the question is very simple. If we open the flood-
gates by allowing the Government servants to join the RSS, let us see what 
will happen to the police officers. If the police is allowed to join the RSS, if 
there is a riot, if there is som e disturbance and there is a crowd on both sides, 
and the police, then we cannot say what will happen. Anything can happen. If 
they are partisan in this sort of thing and they have their own ideas of culture, 
then anything can happen to the persons in unif orm who are in the RSS.  
Even among the bureaucrats, there are two types; those who are
